A comprehensive field study on the Eurasian coot (Fulica atra) conducted in the Danube delta during the 2021 breeding season provided a detailed look at early life-history traits. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] required an average of 22.5 days [ab = 22.5 days] to hatch, a figure that falls squarely within the broader range of 21 to 26 days reported in previous handbooks. Newly hatched chicks weighed approximately 22.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 22.5 grams], a neonatal mass that appears modest relative to the species' ultimate adult dimensions. The initial egg weight before incubation is 36.5 grams [Ww0 = 36.5 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk investment typical of rallids, providing a crucial energy reserve during the first days of post-hatching development. The downy chicks are highly precocial, leaving the nest within hours to forage alongside their parents, though they continue to receive parental brooding during cold spells.

The attainment of flight capability, or fledging, represents a critical developmental milestone in juvenile Eurasian coots. Under the consistently warm thermal conditions of the breeding season, during which water and air temperatures commonly reach 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], young birds achieve their first sustained flight at approximately 57.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 57.5 days after hatching]. This value aligns well with the previously published range of 55 to 60 days, suggesting minimal geographic variation in this trait. Following fledging, the young remain dependent on their parents for several weeks before achieving full nutritional independence. The subsequent transition to the juvenile stage is marked by a steady increase in body mass as individuals refine their foraging skills on aquatic invertebrates and plant material, gradually approaching the adult mass that will be attained by the end of their first year.

Patterns of somatic growth in Eurasian coots are characterized by marked sexual size dimorphism, with adult males regularly attaining a greater asymptotic mass than their female counterparts. The ultimate wet weight for males reaches approximately 835 grams [Wwi = approximately 835 grams], whereas the ultimate wet weight for females is comparatively lower at 715 grams [Wwi = 715 grams]. This 14% difference in adult body mass is consistent with the pattern of reversed sexual size dimorphism observed across many rallid species, likely driven by intrasexual competition among males for access to breeding territories. The growth trajectory from the neonatal mass of 36.5 grams [Ww0 = 36.5 grams] to these adult dimensions is steep during the first two months, followed by a gradual deceleration as the birds approach skeletal maturity in their first autumn and winter.

Reproductive physiology in the Eurasian coot follows a tightly seasonal schedule, governed largely by photoperiod and temperature cues. Sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, occurs at approximately 173 days after hatching [tp = approximately 173 days after hatching] under typical ambient spring temperatures of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This post-hatching interval to puberty is relatively protracted for a bird of this size, likely reflecting the extended period required to acquire the body condition necessary for successful reproduction. The first breeding event, however, occurs somewhat later, with the time since birth at first brood estimated at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], or roughly one year after hatching, under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This delay between physiological puberty and first reproduction suggests that social factors, including territory establishment and pair formation, impose an additional constraint on reproductive onset.

The energetic underpinnings of the coot's active lifestyle are revealed by respirometry measurements conducted on free-living adults. Under standard metabolic conditions at an ambient temperature of 40.0 °C [T = 40.0 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate was recorded at 368 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 368 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, typical for a waterbird of this body mass, reflects the costs of thermoregulation in an aquatic environment. The species' maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the product of clutch size and clutch frequency, is substantial. Females typically lay a single egg per day until the clutch is complete, producing clutches of 8 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 8 eggs per nest], and in productive years they may raise a single brood per breeding season [F_R_i = single brood per breeding season] at the same thermal conditions. The oldest documented individual in a long-term ringing study in the Netherlands reached an age of 32.3 years [am = 32.3 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], representing an exceptional longevity for a rallid and highlighting the species' capacity for delayed senescence.
